title: Weekend Listen: In Defense of Melania
description_html:
As US journalist Azadeh Moaveni was writing her latest book, ‘The East Wing’, a history of America's first ladies and their staff, President Donald Trump’s demolition of that very part of the White House was underway. 

Moaveni presents her book as a “parallel women’s history,” tracing how the wives of US presidents, including Melania Trump, who traditionally had offices in the now-vanished annex, helped shape alliances at home and abroad.

cues.t: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
Podcasts.
Radio.
News.
I took this job in the States and I thought, well, what are the wives of the big powerful men doing here?
First ladies learned that they needed to try to be apolitically political.
There had to be a whole narrative about what they were doing that made it seem about.
Soft power, about values.
Azadeh Mouaveni, known for her journalism on the Middle East and now turning her eye to Washington.
Melania Trump, do you have a sense of her being a different first lady in this second chance she has at the role?
I think she is partly misunderstood.
And I don't think that the public really has a sense of the things that she is committing her time to that have actually been quite significant.
From Bloomberg Weekend, this is The Michelle Hussain Show.
I'm Michelle Hussain.

I've known of Azadeh Muavani's work for a number of years, first from her memoir of growing up Iranian-American and later going to Tehran to work as a journalist, and then her wider reporting and writing on the Middle East, including writing about the women of ISIS.
She is, I think, the only person who has really examined the stories of the women who made that choice, what attracted them and the consequences.

Given all of that expertise, I was intrigued to discover that her forthcoming book is about the United States and specifically about women living close to the heart of power in Washington and indeed exercising it themselves.

The book is called The East Wing, about the first ladies of the last 90 years and the women who worked for them, helping to shape their role as well as their image and therefore the impact they could have.

From Eleanor Roosevelt all the way to Melania Trump, this is a tale of influence and international affairs and one that takes us from Washington right around the world and from the Cold War... all the way to today's Iran war.
As ever, my written notes are a place where you can find the context beyond this conversation, and there is a link to those in the show notes.

Azad and I were both conscious as we spoke that the actual East Wing, the place where First Ladies have traditionally had their offices, has now been bulldozed to make way for President Trump's new ballroom.
And you will hear us talk about that early on.
So, Let's dive in.
Here's what happened when Azadeh Moaveni came into the New York studio to talk to me.
So, of course, Azadeh, I'm interested in your broader thoughts, obviously, at a moment like this, because this has been such a seismic year.
It has. It has, yes.
I actually took on this book project because I thought, oh, well, Iran is very quiet.
Let me explore a different milieu for my themes and got started on this.
And then, of course...
It turned into a big.
Turned.
Into like the big next war.
Yeah. What first got you interested in the stories of the first ladies and their staffers?
Was it one of those that's percolating for a long time or was there a particular moment that started you off?
You know, it was not a particular moment so much as working on that exact same approach, but in a different context.

Before I was working in Lebanon, writing a report about how the UN had a plan to try and diffuse the conflict in Lebanon by bringing together the wives of all the big political leaders and warlords and all the big sort of sect leaders.
So it was very much focused on the wives, recognizing them as influential.
And then I took this job in New York and I landed, you know, in the States and I needed to work on something that was U.S.
Based.
And I thought, well, what are the wives of the big powerful men doing here?
And then actually saw that they're not really written about in a very sort of political way.
They're sort of covered as celebrities or there's biographies of them, of course, but sort of looking at them as almost in the way that we would look at the queen mother and monarchial systems.
They have a lot of power through their familial linkage to the throne.
They're in the presidency and in the key place.
And I also like the way you foreground the staffers as well, because they are really even more... hidden, if you like, behind the scenes.

They're completely, I believe, unobserved in history, even though the chiefs of staff of the president are superstars, there are documentaries about them, there are books about them, and there's a lore about the chief and the chief is this and, you know, he's handed down and they get together and they're so the object of attention as the kind of engine that runs the presidency.
And they generally wanted the credit as well.
They've like claimed their influence, which I think the women around the first ladies, you say early on that they're much less likely to do that.
They shun it.
It was very hard to interview many of them and to ask them whose idea was this?
This was a breakthrough.
This was a diplomatic coup in the Cold War.
And they were they were They would, well, you know, it was me, but it was really they want to credit the principal.
They're very discreet in a way that, yes, the chiefs of the White House are not at all.
And is some of that because in the earlier period you're talking about, they are hired as social secretaries and their job is seen as ceremonial or glossy rather than political or diplomatic?
Well, that's certainly an element of it because their titles don't reflect the influence that they wield and really what they do.
Even the social secretary is still called the social secretary, even though it's really a job that is fundraising and political and diplomatic.
So their titles obscure their influence, certainly.
And It took them a long time to be able to fight in the 60s and 70s to be able to have this role in the executive and sit on the team with the president, the Domestic Policy Council.
There was that arc of trying to be a part of the running of the executive, get the titles to align with what they were doing.
But even then, I think there is a built in deference, protectiveness and discretion amongst the women who work for the first lady.
But now we have a female chief of staff to the president, right?
Susie Riles in a uniquely powerful position.
It's extraordinary.
It's extraordinary that she is the first and that she is the first in this presidency that is breaking all of these democratic norms and battling.
Down these guardrails.

But yet she is the most effective chief of staff that Trump has ever had. but doesn't really see herself as there to advance any kind of women's agenda, which is the chiefs and the staff of the first ladies for many decades felt that that was part of why they were there.

So, of course, Azadeh, I'm really struck by the fact that your book is called The East Wing, and it comes out at exactly the moment when the actual East Wing, the bit of the White House that is home to the first lady's office, is a pile of rubble.
It was quite a shock for me as I was writing this book that that happened, because certainly I was not expecting it.

And I set out to interview all the very elderly, wonderful ladies who had worked for these first ladies over the years, going back to the Kennedy era and the era of Lady Bird Johnson, never imagining that the East Wing itself as a structure would be in any jeopardy.
I saved that for the very end of my research, and it was demolished completely.
October 20th of last year without any notice.
Are you one of those who saw that as something bigger than the plan for the White House ballroom, who saw it as a slight on the role of the First Lady herself?
I think many of the women who worked for First Ladies in the past certainly felt that that was, they felt that way.
They felt slighted because the East Wing is synonymous with their office.
And it has been a sea of women's history.

We found out later that the White House Historical Association, which is charged with looking after the White House since the era of Jackie Kennedy, had gone around and taken pictures and preserved in an almost archaeological way all of the offices where they had worked.
But I believe that the way that it was done, not announced, without public consultation, no one knew.
I mean, the public learned when these shocking images of the bulldozers, you know, crashing into the building surfaced on social media.

So there was a sort of, there was almost a violence to the way that the public learned of it that seemed... insensitive to the profound importance of this place in the history of the White House for women.
Do we know if it was run past Melania Trump?
What's your sense of whether she is fine with this, is happy for her office to be elsewhere?
It has been.
Reportedly been revealed or acknowledged that she was unhappy with it.
But that's all.
She hasn't come out in defense of it, not even once, not in a way that would suggest that she understands the need for the ballroom and she supports the president's plan.
She hasn't lent her support and her credibility to the project.
Do you have a sense of her being a different first lady in this Second chance she has at the role, like how present is she even in Washington?
I mean, I think it took quite a number of months for her to really take up. residence.
I think her second term is completely different than her first.
And she acknowledges it herself.
Like it is for everyone in the White House.
Indeed, indeed.
In her documentary, Melania, she's actually very self-aware about the importance of her second term being different.
She interviews on camera women for her East Wing office and asks them, you know, with a kind of raised eyebrow, how do you think that my second term office should be different than my first?
So she's not in residence much, we understand, but she actually is much more deliberate.
She has more serious staff.
She has a small staff, but she has serious staff.
Doing what?
Well, she.
came in with actually a real, with a real win.
She helped push through the Take It Down Act, which was a bipartisan bill in Congress that criminalizes deepfake and revenge porn, which is something that's certainly impacting young women.
And I think it's been a very long time since the First Lady's been able to push through a really critical piece of legislation in Congress.
So I think she is partly misunderstood.
I think she shuns the attention of what she would call the mainstream media because she thinks that it slights her and doesn't take her seriously.
And I don't think that the public really has a sense of the things that she is committing her time to that have actually been quite significant.

The story you tell in The East Wing is, of course, a much longer one, over 125 years, and you cast it as a parallel women's history, not only the first ladies themselves, but the women working for them.
And I guess going back to the beginning, it is really Eleanor Roosevelt in the 1930s who.
Strikes out in a new way and is the first lady that no one can ignore?
She's the one who really creates the role as this influential partner to the president, this interpreter of America's maladies, this mirror to the nation.
She's a peace activist.
She's a diplomat.
She's the envoy for FDR.
She is a champion for women.
She institutes these women's only press conferences because she wants women reporters to be able to get on the front page and to be taken seriously in newsrooms.
So she trailblazes.

But she does that, you know, completely on her own, essentially, with the with the aid of one staffer, Malvina Thompson, who's an important character in this because they're a team. you know, how did Eleanor Roosevelt manage to be Eleanor Roosevelt?
And that's when the office story begins.
She has a profound international legacy.
You know, she's part of the international post-World War II, a shaper of that whole order.
It's interesting, though, that 60 years later, when Hillary Clinton is coming into the White House as First Lady, she, I mean, Eleanor Roosevelt is her big role model.
She kind of thinks that she can act in that image.
And it's like, America's not really ready for that in the 90s.
America was not ready for that in the 90s.
Maybe it still isn't ready for it, arguably.
It may not still be ready for it.
I mean, Eleanor Roosevelt was of her time, of course.
I think the Second World War and what the country was going through with the Great Depression.
I think in.

The 90s, you know, Hillary Clinton went about her life incredibly politically ambitious health care agenda in a way that was perhaps not as anticipatory of the way that Americans expected the first lady to essentially hide and soften her political ambitions and value, even on behalf of the president's agenda.
So she went too fast.
I don't know if she went too fast.
I think that she was perhaps too explicit.
I think what first ladies learned after that whole experience of Hillary Clinton's with health care is that they needed to try to.
Be apolitically political.
It had to be softened.
There had to be a whole narrative about what they were doing that made it seem.
About soft power, about values.
There had to be a story.

You know, Michelle Obama, I think, is the sort of the successful version of a first lady who wanted to transform in even a legislative way an aspect of Americans' health care, childhood obesity, but went about it seeming as though she was planting a White House garden and, you know, carrying the nation along with just a different, more healthy way to live.
But it's still a safer issue, isn't it?
Like, you know, eating healthily. is a safe issue compared to actually health care and tackling that system in America.
And that has been the theme.
I guess in that sense, you can see Melania Trump is probably being a bit braver.
She is a bit braver, I would say, in some ways.

I mean, up to the Reagan era, first ladies in a kind of bipartisan way, Republican first ladies, Democratic first ladies could take on projects and politics that related to women's equality and women's rights and the role of women in this country in a way that was not dangerous to their husbands' electoral prospects.
I mean, Betty Ford supported the Equal Rights Amendment.
Pat Nixon was critical to getting more women appointed into the federal government.
In the 90s, America was changing and we had the rise of evangelical Christianity and religion, traditional gender roles became an element in politics in a way that it hadn't before.
And so that really constrained what the first lady could focus on and attempt to do in terms of her projects and her politics.
So there was a shrinking.
So they always have to operate in the context of their times.
I want to pick out another very famous first lady, because I think you portray something that is not really recognized about her.
Jackie Kennedy is known, of course, for her style, her charm, her love of the arts.
But you do show that she too has diplomatic achievements.
She is such a superstar of her time and is remembered as such a queen of America, of Kamala.
Yes, her incredible diplomatic ambition and sensitivity and shrewdness is sort of, I think, almost lost to her story.
She worked closely with the social secretary, press secretary, Tish Baldrige, who was also wanted to be a diplomat. but she couldn't go into the diplomatic corps at the time because it was the 60s.
So between the two of them, in this incredibly subtle way, they turned their political entertaining into an element of the Kennedy administration's foreign policy during the Cold War.
Particularly in relation to India and Pakistan at the beginning of the 60s.
She turned around America's relationship, certainly with India, because Prime Minister Nehru was very distant towards the Kennedy administration.
He felt that Kennedy was a young sort of debonair, perhaps.
He didn't take him terribly seriously, but he was really drawn to Jackie Kennedy and her sister.
And so Jackie gets dispatched by the U.S. government as essentially the envoy to India and Pakistan.
And she goes and she has this mesmerizing tour that's covered around the world.
And Nehru keeps a picture of her in his office forever after.
So she does.
She's sort of the one who's able to seal the relationship.

Interesting. And I was also, I have a bit of a personal connection to one thing you write about, which is that before Jackie Kennedy goes to India and Pakistan, there's this very high profile visit of Ayub Khan, the president of Pakistan, to Washington.
And there's a big dinner at Mount Vernon.
Yes.
And Ayub Khan's first lady was, was his daughter.
She acted as his first lady in that time.
And I looked up the pictures of this dinner at Mount Vernon and there is Yubran's daughter Nassim in her sari.
My grandmother was the person who taught her to wear a sari.
So helped prepare her for her role as the first lady of Pakistan.
It is remembered by historians and scholars of first ladies.
It is par excellence the most iconic, elaborate, creative pageantry of state dinner ever.
I mean, they sailed down the Potomac River to Mount Vernon at dusk.
They had orchestras on the banks.
I mean, it's unparalleled.
There's been nothing like it since.
Extraordinary. I'd love to talk a bit about your lens on all of this as an Iranian American, Azadeh, because you've written about your own heritage.
You've reported from and on the Middle East for 25 years.
There is a moment when I think your worlds intersect in this book because Jackie Kennedy at one point was nearly outshone by the Empress of Iran when she came to the White House.
Yes.
But managed to hold her own.
She managed to hold her own.
Empress Farah at the time was, after Jackie or perhaps alongside Jackie, the most sort of celebrated, sophisticated royal or first.
Lady in the world.
So when the Shah and the Empress came to Washington, it was a sort of style showdown for the two of them.
And the President Kennedy teased Jackie, you know, you should get your jewels out.
You need to make sure that, you know, the Empress doesn't outshine you.

So it was fun to see how both of them in their own times, quite tremendous in their roles, but being watched on the world stage to see who for the sort of glory of their nation was the most sparkling, you know, woman on the stage.
Obviously, it was a different time for Iran.
So then bring us up to the present day and this extraordinary year between Iran and the United States.
I mean, you must feel it as well as have to analyze it.
What do you think you have learned in the course of seeing what has played out this year that you didn't expect?
I didn't expect Iranians to turn out in January.
Against the regime.
Against the regime in the way that they did.
I mean, I've been covering Iran for, I mean, it's getting close to 30 years now.

And of course, they've been frustrated and impoverished and angry for many, many years now and have managed to, you know, carve out space for themselves to have more civil liberties and social liberties through their own kind of civil disobedience campaigns, the Women Life Freedom Movement that really sort of ended dress codes in Iran.
But I didn't expect them to respond to the call of Crown Prince-in-Exile Reza Pahlavi, because for years we've covered him, you know,

those of us who covered the Iraq War and saw that the role of the diaspora can be overimagined by politicians and it can be very risky to put any hopes on a diaspora leader to be part of an agenda, military or otherwise, for change, you know, in their home country.
I didn't expect them to turn out you know, in the way that they did filling the streets of these cities across the country.
And then, of course, the war began.
So what are your conclusions now about what that movement in January could have grown into in different circumstances?

It's a very, it's a very good question, because the few weeks in between, I think we almost forget about them, that Iran went quite rapidly from a massacre, like a terrible massacre, I think, in 48 hours.
The numbers are disputed, but even the accounts of five, six, 7,000, I mean, these are tremendous killed.
By the regime.

I think that had there been any kind of military intervention or the assassination of the Supreme Leader or any kind of sort of move towards war much earlier, I think that the Islamic Republic might have really teetered because people.
Were on the brink.
They were on the edge and it looked like things could collapse.
But the weeks in between, you know, people came to understand the scale of of the atrocities that frightened them. you know,

this is a country that went through this profound trauma of these massacres that have no precedent in living memory and was coping with that and figuring out how to, you know, even countenance or think about its relationship with the system and the aftermath of that and then this war.
Because President Trump did say at the time of those protests, help is on the way.

You're suggesting that the mood changed then in the intervening weeks, although you still have the The reality that however much people feel against their own government, being bombed by outsiders can just be something that is then beyond the pale for people.
Both of those things.
I mean, he promised the help was on the way and it was not on the way.
People were not aided or assisted.

You know, whether they ultimately would have would have wanted that, I don't know. because to have your regime changed or your system changed through an assault and through a foreign intervention is something that people, I think, everywhere would be deeply ambivalent about.

But there were many people who saw no other way, who saw no other way for things to move, that the Islamic Republic's security apparatus holds so much power and is so repressive that without some kind of outside help, there would be no way to dislodge it and to get the country out of its current impasse.
But then The war didn't turn out to be just a war of decapitation, striking military sites and targets of the regime.
It very quickly became a war against all of Iran.
There were civilian infrastructure hit.
There was a school in Minab that was hit.
So many of those people who at the outset thought, oh, well, perhaps this will save us, saw that this was not just a war against the the regime, but a war against the whole country.
So when you were there recently, did you feel that the regime was stronger than the last time you were there?
I think people's willingness to sort of continue to give the system credit in the way that they did in the aftermath of April and May, I would say is on the wane.

You know, when the war was against Tehran, those 40 days when Tehran was being bombarded, I think there was a real kind of seizing up of nationalism, of a sense that this was a system for, you know, everything else that it had done was defending the country.
It kept the country secure.
It kept the capital secure.
It kept the borders relatively secure.
And I think that it softened people's attitudes or it gave them a sort of gratefulness.
But that has really started to.
Evaporate because they were relieved that this memorandum of understanding was signed by the U.S., And now.
Watch what the regime is doing.
They see that it started firing on ships in the Persian Gulf, that it was sort of seeking out provocation again.
So I think now the mood has shifted once again towards anger and frustration.
You defended us well.
You know, now go back to the negotiating table, make some concessions.
You know, we want this war to end.
People are exhausted of no war, no peace.
And this regime seems like it can you know, deliver some war, but it can't deliver peace.
Do you think Reza Pahlavi could still be the one?
Do you think he could be a future leader or has that moment passed?
The moment passed.
The moment passed.
There was much hope in him and he performed really badly.
Because? He was never able to.
Walk the line of being a nationalistic protector of the country.
He was never able to say, I don't want my country to be attacked.
I am worried for the state of my country.
I mourn when my compatriots are killed in U.S.
Attacks. He was he.

Allied himself in such a crude way with the Israelis, I think, in a way that worried people and turned them off. he was just never really able to seize the moment and have the kind of charisma and leadership and empathy that people were looking to him for.
And so I think he was seen as someone who was just abetting the destruction from the outside.

So I'd love to know your thoughts about the region more widely, because you've not only reported from Iran, but you've seen the aftermath of the Iraq War in the early 2000s, the so-called Arab Spring, the rise of ISIS.
You wrote a book about the women who joined ISIS.

How would you characterize the development or otherwise of women in the region, I guess, from the period of the Islamic Revolution, when women were part of bringing Ayatollah Khomeini to power in Iran?
Women have been really at the forefront of all of these movements of the last...

50 years, even the very violent and seemingly quite fundamentalist movements, sort of seeing in this kind of anti-Western embrace of orthodox Islam, a sort of language or a style of resistance to the West.
And often that's been in sort of backlash or reaction to secular dictators who've used women's rights and secular codes for women.
You know, that has been seen as part of their authoritarian ethos.

I'd love you to explain that a bit more, because I think it's really striking that these, you're thinking about places like Tunisia or Bashar al-Assad, who are you know, leaders who are Muslims, but secular, but political rights don't stem from that.
No, exactly.

So whether it's Iran in the late 70s, under the Shah, or Tunisia under the Ben Ali dictatorship, which was, you know, the secular dictatorship that was overthrown by the revolution in Tunisia during the Arab Spring, Bashar al-Assad, even the Egyptian order that was challenged by the Muslim Brotherhood, the Tahrir Revolution, the Arab Spring, women were very much at the vanguard of those protests.
And they embraced.
Islamism, jihadism, eventually, and this very regressive, uninclusive spirit in order to bring them down.

And that's partly because, I mean, perhaps, you know, this is now becoming very nerdy, Michelle, but place to place, women became part of these militant movements, imagining that once they succeeded, they would be included and that they would have a place at the table and that they would be part of the new order.
And that did not come to be the case, which is why women in large numbers from the Arab world joined the Islamic State.
And women from the Western world.
That perhaps is harder to explain, including some very young women, people like Shamima Begum, who was 15 when she left the UK.
So what is the attraction there?
I'm conscious that, and you bring this out in Guesthouse for Young Widows, that there are many complex circumstances.
And sometimes women are leaving their husbands and escaping to Islamic State.
And sometimes there are all kinds of other reasons.
But how do you explain people like Shamima Begum, who've grown up with every possibility of succeeding on their own terms in the West?
I think these young women from European countries, from Western countries, were groomed and trafficked.
Because They didn't go in huge numbers, ultimately.
So this wasn't sort of about the domestic politics of France or the United Kingdom.

I think that ISIS was very skillful and spent a lot of money and resources in its propaganda directed country to country, trying to prey on the racial and cultural insecurities of second generation Muslims.

So it really devoted this kind of bespoke propaganda to schoolgirls in London who were the daughters of conservative you know, Muslim origin families who didn't feel like they belonged, who felt like their parents didn't understand them, who felt that they were not accepted in British society.
And this group came in cunningly with a strategy for them.
I mean, it was so specific.
You could sort of imagine, you know, a very polished marketing outfit creating that for them.
And then they surrounded them with people on the ground in East London, in Bradford, in Luton, wherever, who were also able to be part of what was essentially a whole grooming agenda.
So the caliphate becomes like a promised land almost.
The caliphate to them became a promised land.
It was a place where they could be active as women, but they could also wear their hijabs and they could be religious and they wouldn't be looked down upon.
They wouldn't be frowned upon as backwards.
They would fit somewhere and they would make a difference.
So these were teenagers, I think, being seduced to join this kind of utopian place where they would have a role.

Let's just to close, like talk about the Middle East and the US more broadly, Azadeh, because there's a lot of discussion and debate about the future of the US presence in the region and what happens to bases, but more widely, the extent to which the US is going to stay involved.
I mean, Donald Trump was a president who said no more wars.
And he is the one who has taken the US into another war in the Middle East.
So what do you think the future looks like? for the relationship between the U.S. and the region?
The relationship between the U.S.

And the region will be fundamentally altered in ways that we might not see in an immediate one to two year horizon, because I think all of the big regional players sort of see that they have to wait out this Trump presidency because he's taken America into a war that he cannot extricate the country from.

But I think fundamentally within the region, you know, big players, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkey. the Persian Gulf monarchies who believed that they could rely on the U.S. security umbrella, now see that they cannot, and that also that this war, the Israeli-American war, has destabilized their economies, it's destabilized their growth models.

And so there will have to be, and there's talk of it already, between the Gulf countries, Iran and Turkey, looking to a whole new regional paradigm. where these countries, because of their geography, have to come to a new kind of security alignment or posture or accommodation with one another that will not make them.
Vulnerable to the old setup.
Because the old setup was meant at very high cost to deliver security to the Arab countries of the Gulf, but has actually just made them terribly vulnerable.
So now they see Iran as a neighbor that they must somehow accommodate in terms of security.
So do you think the push will come from them, from those Gulf countries, like, you know, the big bases in Qatar?
Bahrain, in Saudi Arabia.
Do you think that they will want those to come to an end rather than the US decide it doesn't want to have that kind of presence?
Well, maybe it's mutual.
Maybe it is mutual.
I mean, the bases have been shown to be very hard to defend.
And for these countries, you know, what is the utility of these bases if they are actually making Qatar vulnerable, if they're making.
The UAE vulnerable?

From the other side, though, I mean, to extricate themselves from this relationship with the United States is also extremely costly because, you know, these are countries that are you know, client states, essentially.
I mean, they don't hold elections.
They are not representative.
They rely on the United States in many ways to sort of keep them in power.
And they also obviously want the economic relationship with the United States.
They do want the economic relationship, but they buy arms, you know, buy the billions, arms that don't, I mean, they're not using these arms to protect themselves.
So they pay protection money and aren't being protected anymore.
And having these bases, you know, in the case of the UAE, endangers their entire sort of stability expat oasis model.
So I think we're in a time of tremendous transition.
You know, will we see the bases dwindle, disappear?
Will we see demands made?
I think all of these countries are sort of refining and thinking through how they can accommodate being squeezed between Iran and the US in a way that they never expected to find themselves.
And what have these months of the war been like for you as an Iranian-American?
We had Vali Nasser on the show right at the beginning of the war, and he said it's just, there are such deep fractures in the diaspora community.
He actually said that the community was eating itself.
I think he meant Iranian-Americans, but probably those elsewhere in the world.
What's your sense of it?
Um... It has been a very painful time because I think, you know, the Iranian diaspora is no exception.

Many diasporas, you know, become so out of touch in ways with the story of or the experience of the suffering of people back in the homeland that their politics almost detach and become a politics specific to that diaspora.
Maybe Cuban Americans are similar.
So it is terribly divided.
I mean, people, families falling out.

I think most Iranians inside Iran are angry at the United States for attacking their country, but they do not see the United States as a reason for why Iran is in the dreadful, dreadful hole that it's in.
They blame the Islamic Republic.
They hold the Islamic Republic accountable.
But when you sort of read and circulate in the diaspora, I mean, they're just like American leftists.
They're anti-imperial. They're angry at the United States.
I mean, the United States is not ultimately responsible for the welfare of Iranians.
The Iranian leaders.
Are responsible for the welfare of Iranians.
Azadeh Moaveni, thank you so much.
Congratulations on the East Wing.
Thank you. Thank you, Michelle.
It's been good to talk to you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So whether it's Iran in the late 70s, under the Shah, or Tunisia under the Ben Ali dictatorship, which was, you know, the secular dictatorship that was overthrown by the revolution in Tunisia during the Arab Spring, Bashar al-Assad, even the Egyptian order that was challenged by the Muslim Brotherhood, the Tahrir Revolution, the Arab Spring, women were very much at the vanguard of those protests.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And they embraced.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Islamism, jihadism, eventually, and this very regressive, uninclusive spirit in order to bring them down. And that's partly because, I mean, perhaps, you know, this is now becoming very nerdy, Michelle, but place to place, women became part of these militant movements, imagining that once they succeeded, they would be included and that they would have a place at the table and that they would be part of the new order.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And that did not come to be the case, which is why women in large numbers from the Arab world joined the Islamic State.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And women from the Western world. That perhaps is harder to explain, including some very young women, people like Shamima Begum, who was 15 when she left the UK. So what is the attraction there? I'm conscious that, and you bring this out in Guesthouse for Young Widows, that there are many complex circumstances. And sometimes women are leaving their husbands and escaping to Islamic State. And sometimes there are all kinds of other reasons.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But how do you explain people like Shamima Begum, who've grown up with every possibility of succeeding on their own terms in the West?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think these young women from European countries, from Western countries, were groomed and trafficked. Because They didn't go in huge numbers, ultimately. So this wasn't sort of about the domestic politics of France or the United Kingdom. I think that ISIS was very skillful and spent a lot of money and resources in its propaganda directed country to country, trying to prey on the racial and cultural insecurities of second generation Muslims.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So it really devoted this kind of bespoke propaganda to schoolgirls in London who were the daughters of conservative you know, Muslim origin families who didn't feel like they belonged, who felt like their parents didn't understand them, who felt that they were not accepted in British society. And this group came in cunningly with a strategy for them. I mean, it was so specific. You could sort of imagine, you know, a very polished marketing outfit creating that for them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And then they surrounded them with people on the ground in East London, in Bradford, in Luton, wherever, who were also able to be part of what was essentially a whole grooming agenda.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the caliphate becomes like a promised land almost.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The caliphate to them became a promised land.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It was a place where they could be active as women, but they could also wear their hijabs and they could be religious and they wouldn't be looked down upon. They wouldn't be frowned upon as backwards. They would fit somewhere and they would make a difference. So these were teenagers, I think, being seduced to join this kind of utopian place where they would have a role.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Let's just to close, like talk about the Middle East and the US more broadly, Azadeh, because there's a lot of discussion and debate about the future of the US presence in the region and what happens to bases, but more widely, the extent to which the US is going to stay involved. I mean, Donald Trump was a president who said no more wars. And he is the one who has taken the US into another war in the Middle East.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So what do you think the future looks like? for the relationship between the U.S. and the region?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The relationship between the U.S.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And the region will be fundamentally altered in ways that we might not see in an immediate one to two year horizon, because I think all of the big regional players sort of see that they have to wait out this Trump presidency because he's taken America into a war that he cannot extricate the country from. But I think fundamentally within the region, you know, big players, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkey. the Persian Gulf monarchies who believed that they could rely on the U.S. security umbrella, now see that they cannot, and that also that this war, the Israeli-American war, has destabilized their economies, it's destabilized their growth models.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And so there will have to be, and there's talk of it already, between the Gulf countries, Iran and Turkey, looking to a whole new regional paradigm. where these countries, because of their geography, have to come to a new kind of security alignment or posture or accommodation with one another that will not make them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Vulnerable to the old setup.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Because the old setup was meant at very high cost to deliver security to the Arab countries of the Gulf, but has actually just made them terribly vulnerable. So now they see Iran as a neighbor that they must somehow accommodate in terms of security.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So do you think the push will come from them, from those Gulf countries, like, you know, the big bases in Qatar? Bahrain, in Saudi Arabia. Do you think that they will want those to come to an end rather than the US decide it doesn't want to have that kind of presence?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Well, maybe it's mutual. Maybe it is mutual. I mean, the bases have been shown to be very hard to defend. And for these countries, you know, what is the utility of these bases if they are actually making Qatar vulnerable, if they're making.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The UAE vulnerable?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: From the other side, though, I mean, to extricate themselves from this relationship with the United States is also extremely costly because, you know, these are countries that are you know, client states, essentially. I mean, they don't hold elections. They are not representative. They rely on the United States in many ways to sort of keep them in power.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And they also obviously want the economic relationship with the United States.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They do want the economic relationship, but they buy arms, you know, buy the billions, arms that don't, I mean, they're not using these arms to protect themselves. So they pay protection money and aren't being protected anymore. And having these bases, you know, in the case of the UAE, endangers their entire sort of stability expat oasis model. So I think we're in a time of tremendous transition. You know, will we see the bases dwindle, disappear?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Will we see demands made? I think all of these countries are sort of refining and thinking through how they can accommodate being squeezed between Iran and the US in a way that they never expected to find themselves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And what have these months of the war been like for you as an Iranian-American? We had Vali Nasser on the show right at the beginning of the war, and he said it's just, there are such deep fractures in the diaspora community. He actually said that the community was eating itself. I think he meant Iranian-Americans, but probably those elsewhere in the world. What's your sense of it?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Um... It has been a very painful time because I think, you know, the Iranian diaspora is no exception. Many diasporas, you know, become so out of touch in ways with the story of or the experience of the suffering of people back in the homeland that their politics almost detach and become a politics specific to that diaspora. Maybe Cuban Americans are similar. So it is terribly divided. I mean, people, families falling out.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think most Iranians inside Iran are angry at the United States for attacking their country, but they do not see the United States as a reason for why Iran is in the dreadful, dreadful hole that it's in. They blame the Islamic Republic. They hold the Islamic Republic accountable. But when you sort of read and circulate in the diaspora, I mean, they're just like American leftists. They're anti-imperial. They're angry at the United States.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I mean, the United States is not ultimately responsible for the welfare of Iranians.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The Iranian leaders.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Are responsible for the welfare of Iranians.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Azadeh Moaveni, thank you so much. Congratulations on the East Wing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you, Michelle.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's been good to talk to you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It's been wonderful. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And that's where we left it. But if you'd like to know more about Azadeh's wider work and indeed read my own reflections on the conversation, don't forget those written notes, which you can find at bloomberg.com forward slash Michelle. We publish them with every episode. And so to the team, the show's producers are Jessica Beck and Chris Martlew. The video, because you can watch this conversation in full, is produced and edited by Andy Hayward.

segments.text: Guest booking is by Elan Bird. Social media by Alex Morgan. Production assistance from Indira Ray. Our music is by Bart Warshaw. And the executive producer is Louisa Lewis. For this episode, Cale Brooks was running the studio in New York. And at Bloomberg Weekend, thanks to Brendan Francis Newnham and our executive editor, Catherine Bell. Until the next time, goodbye.

study.one_liner_ko: 저널리스트 아자데 모아베니가 신작 『The East Wing』을 중심으로 영부인과 그 참모들의 숨은 영향력, 멜라니아 트럼프의 재평가, 그리고 이란 전쟁 이후 중동 정세를 이야기한다.
summary_ko: 모아베니는 미국 영부인과 그 여성 참모들을 '평행한 여성의 역사'로 다룬다. 대통령 비서실장들은 스타가 되지만, 영부인 참모들은 공을 영부인에게 돌리고 신중하게 처신해서 역사에서 잘 보이지 않는다.
트럼프가 예고 없이 이스트윙을 철거해 이 책의 출간 시점과 겹쳤다. 과거 영부인 참모들은 모욕감을 느꼈고, 멜라니아도 불만을 가졌다고 알려졌지만 공개적으로 옹호하지는 않았다.
모아베니는 멜라니아가 '부분적으로 오해받고 있다'고 본다. 2기에는 더 의도적으로 움직이고 소규모지만 진지한 참모진을 꾸렸으며, 딥페이크·리벤지 포르노를 처벌하는 Take It Down Act를 통과시킨 성과가 있다고 한다.
엘eanor 루스벨트가 영부인 역할을 만들었고, 힐러리 클린턴은 지나치게 정치적으로 드러나 반발을 샀다. 이후 영부인들은 '비정치적으로 정치적'이어야 했고, 미셸 오바마의 텃밭 캠페인이 성공 사례다. 재키 케네디는 인도·파키스탄 외교에서 숨은 역할을 했다.
이란 이야기에서는 1월 대규모 시위, 대학살, 이후 전쟁이 시민 정서를 어떻게 바꿨는지 짚는다. 레자 팔라비는 기회를 놓쳤다고 평가한다. 걸프 국가들은 미국 안보 우산에 대한 믿음이 흔들려 새로운 지역 안보 질서를 모색하고 있다.
여성들이 중동의 혁명·급진 운동 전면에 있었던 이유와, 서구 소녀들이 ISIS에 끌려간 과정(그루밍·맞춤형 선전)도 설명한다. 이란 디아스포라의 분열과 책임 소재에 대한 생각으로 마무리한다.
study.summary_en: This one's an interview with Azadeh Moaveni about her new book on America's first ladies and the women who worked for them. Her point is that those staffers shaped diplomacy but almost never took the credit, while the chiefs of staff became celebrities. Timing-wise, Trump bulldozed the actual East Wing without warning, which she found pretty shocking. She also argues Melania is partly misunderstood and pushed through a real law. Then it turns to Iran: the January protests, the war, why Reza Pahlavi missed his moment, and how Gulf states are rethinking their reliance on the US security umbrella.

expressions.nuance_ko: 일부러 모순어법(oxymoron)을 써서 이중적 상황을 한마디로 압축하는 수사법이다. 'X-ly Y' 형태로 응용하면 토론에서 인상적으로 들린다. 약간 분석적이고 냉소적인 톤이다.
examples: Our CEO has to be apolitically political: take a stand on the issue, but never name a party.
Every office has someone who's apolitically political, always lobbying but calling it just being helpful.
As a diplomat's spouse, you learn to be apolitically political at dinner parties.

similar.example: Journalists walk a fine line between being critical and being partisan.
His answer was strategically ambiguous, so nobody could pin him down.

expressions.quote: But managed to hold her own.
expressions.nuance_ko: 자신보다 강하거나 유명한 상대 앞에서 기죽지 않고 대등하게 해낸다는 칭찬이다. 'hold your own against/with/in'으로 이어 쓴다. 회의·토론·스포츠에서 두루 쓰는 구어체다.
examples: She was the youngest person on the panel, but she held her own against two professors.
My Korean is rusty, but I can hold my own in a business meeting.
The underdog team held its own for the whole first half.

similar.example: He stood his ground even when the whole room disagreed.
I could barely keep up with them on the hike.

expressions.nuance_ko: wield는 power, influence, authority 같은 추상 명사와 어울리는 격식 있는 동사다. 'a lot of power to wield'처럼 큰 힘을 가졌다는 어감이 있다. 뒤에 붙는 관계절 'the influence they wield' 형태가 자연스럽다.
examples: A few big landlords wield enormous influence over this neighborhood.
Be careful how you use the authority you wield as a manager.
Social media creators now wield more sway than many newspapers.

similar.example: Investors are exerting pressure on the board to step down.
Her opinion carries a lot of weight in the committee.

expressions.quote: Walk the line of being a nationalistic protector of the country.
expressions.nuance_ko: 'walk the line of being A (without becoming B)'로 쓰면 줄타기 같은 균형을 표현한다. 'walk a fine/tightrope line'이 더 흔한 변형이다. 정치·리더십·처신을 논할 때 유용하다.
examples: Managers have to walk the line between being friendly and being the boss.
The comedian walked the line of being edgy without being offensive.
It's hard to walk the line between honesty and tact with your in-laws.

similar.example: We need to strike a balance between speed and quality.
The mayor threaded the needle with a compromise both sides accepted.

expressions.nuance_ko: 사회적·도덕적으로 받아들일 수 있는 선을 넘었다는 뜻이다. 'be/go beyond the pale'로 쓰며 다소 격식 있고 단호한 비판이다. 단순히 '싫다'가 아니라 '선을 넘었다'는 느낌이다.
examples: Interrupting a eulogy to take a phone call is beyond the pale.
Some of the comments online went way beyond the pale.
Honestly, charging guests to use the bathroom is beyond the pale.

similar.example: That joke crossed the line.
Personal questions about salary are out of bounds here.

expressions.nuance_ko: 인기·영향력·열기가 서서히 줄어드는 상황에 쓰는 격식 있는 표현이다. 'on the rise'의 반대 짝으로 기억하면 좋다. 보통 be on the wane로 쓰고 급격한 붕괴보다는 완만한 하락을 말한다.
examples: The craze for these fitness trackers seems to be on the wane.
His popularity has been on the wane since the scandal.
Enthusiasm for the project is on the wane, honestly.

similar.example: The campaign started to lose steam in March.
Interest in the show faded out after season two.

expressions.quote: they have to wait out this Trump presidency
expressions.nuance_ko: 행동하지 않고 상황이 지나가길 기다리는 전략적 인내를 나타낸다. 목적어는 폭풍·위기·임기 같은 '끝이 있는 것'이다. 'ride out'과 비슷하지만 wait out은 수동적인 느낌이 더 강하다.
examples: Let's wait out the storm before we drive back.
Some employees just wait out every new reorganization.
I'm going to wait out this market dip instead of selling.

similar.example: The company rode out the recession without layoffs.
Just sit tight until we hear from the client.

expressions.expression: not so much X as Y
expressions.quote: it was not a particular moment so much as working on that exact same approach
expressions.nuance_ko: 흔한 'not X but Y'를 부드럽게 정정하는 틀이다. 질문의 전제를 살짝 바로잡으며 자기 생각을 내세울 때 좋다. 인터뷰·패널 답변의 시작 문구로 자연스럽다.
examples: It's not so much a pay issue as a respect issue.
I didn't leave the job so much as outgrow it.
The delay was not so much bad luck as bad planning.

similar.expression: it's less about X than Y
similar.example: It's less about the money than the principle.

expressions.quote: if it was run past Melania Trump
expressions.nuance_ko: 결정하거나 발표하기 전에 상대의 의견·동의를 비공식적으로 구하는 뜻이다. 업무 대화에서 매우 자주 쓴다. 'Did you run it past legal?'처럼 하면 사전 협의 여부를 따지는 질문이 된다.
examples: Can I run this draft past you before I send it to the client?
Did anyone run the new logo past the marketing team?
I'd like to run an idea past you over lunch.

similar.example: Can I bounce an idea off you real quick?
Let's loop legal in before we announce.

expressions.quote: She hasn't come out in defense of it, not even once
expressions.nuance_ko: 'come out'은 공개적으로 입장을 밝힌다는 뜻이고, in defense of가 옹호를 더한다. 뉴스에서 정치인이 논란에 대해 입장을 낼 때 자주 쓴다. 부정문으로 '침묵하고 있다'는 점을 강조할 수 있다.
examples: No one on the team came out in defense of the manager.
Several actors came out in defense of the director.
He didn't come out in defense of his friend, which hurt.

similar.example: She spoke up for her colleague in the meeting.
The company stood by its decision.

expressions.expression: have a place at the table
expressions.quote: that they would have a place at the table
expressions.nuance_ko: 문자 그대로의 식탁이 아니라 협상·의사결정에 낀다는 비유다. 'have a seat at the table'과 거의 같고, 포용성·대표성 논의에서 자주 쓰인다. 'earn/deserve a place at the table'로도 응용한다.
examples: Younger staff want a place at the table when we plan the strategy.
Small suppliers deserve a place at the table in these talks.
If we're affected by the decision, we should have a place at the table.

similar.expression: have a seat at the table
similar.example: Customers should have a seat at the table when we design the product.
Everyone should have a say in the schedule.

expressions.quote: went about it seeming as though she was planting a White House garden
expressions.nuance_ko: 'go about + ing/명사'는 일을 처리하는 방식과 접근법에 초점을 둔다. 'How did you go about it?'처럼 방법을 묻는 데 쓴다. 결과보다 과정·전략을 말할 때 자연스럽다.
examples: How did you go about negotiating the raise?
She went about the move so quietly that nobody noticed.
I'm not sure how to go about asking for feedback.

similar.example: How would you approach a tough conversation like that?

debate.q: Should unelected spouses and advisers of top leaders have an official, public role?
debate.for: Their influence is real, so formal titles bring transparency and accountability; hiding it just obscures how decisions get made.
debate.against: Nobody voted for them, so formalizing it creates unaccountable power and conflicts of interest; informal influence should stay informal.

debate.q: Is a regional security order built on a foreign great power's protection ultimately a trap for the host countries?
debate.for: Dependence makes host countries targets and limits their policy choices, so they pay protection money and are still vulnerable.
debate.against: Alliances provide real deterrence and economic ties, and leaving them is costly and risky; a vacuum may be more dangerous.

shadowing.reason_ko: 한 인물에 대한 평가를 이유와 함께 차분하게 설명하는 구조라 패널·대화에서 그대로 쓰기 좋다.
'deliver some war, but it can't deliver peace'처럼 대구로 마무리하는 수사가 인상적이고 리듬이 좋다.
긴 문장에서 분석→예측을 이어가는 호흡과 'wait out', 'extricate' 같은 어휘를 연습할 수 있다.

difficulty.note_ko: 인터뷰 대화체이지만 정치·역사·중동 정세 어휘가 많고 문장이 길다. 말끊김과 겹침이 많은 구어 특성에 익숙해지면 패널 토론 표현을 얻기 좋다.

translations_sent.4-4: 미국에서 이 일을 맡게 되면서 이런 생각이 들었어요. 여기서 권력 있는 거물 남성들의 아내들은 대체 뭘 하고 있을까?
translations_sent.5-5: 영부인들은 '정치적이지 않은 방식으로 정치적인' 존재가 되어야 한다는 걸 깨달았죠.
translations_sent.6-6: 자신들이 하는 일이 그렇게 보이도록 만드는 하나의 서사가 통째로 필요했어요.
translations_sent.7-7: 소프트 파워, 그리고 가치에 관한 일이라는 서사요.
translations_sent.8-8: 아자데 무아베니는 중동 관련 저널리즘으로 유명한데, 이제는 워싱턴으로 눈을 돌렸습니다.
translations_sent.9-9: 멜라니아 트럼프의 경우, 두 번째로 이 역할을 맡은 지금은 예전과 다른 영부인이라는 느낌이 드시나요?
translations_sent.10-10: 그녀는 어느 정도 오해받고 있다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.11-11: 그리고 대중이 그녀가 시간을 쏟고 있는 일들, 실제로는 꽤 의미 있는 일들에 대해 제대로 알고 있다고는 생각하지 않아요.
translations_sent.12-12: 블룸버그 위켄드가 전해 드리는 미셸 후세인 쇼입니다.
translations_sent.14-14: 저는 아자데 무아베니의 작업을 몇 년 전부터 알고 있었어요. 처음엔 이란계 미국인으로 자란 이야기를 담은 회고록이었고, 이후 테헤란에 가서 기자로 일한 경험, 그리고 ISIS의 여성들에 관한 글을 포함해 중동 전반에 대한 취재와 집필로 이어졌죠.
translations_sent.15-15: 제가 보기에 그녀는 그런 선택을 한 여성들의 이야기, 무엇이 그들을 끌어당겼고 어떤 결과가 따랐는지를 제대로 파헤친 유일한 사람이에요.
translations_sent.16-16: 그런 전문성을 생각하면, 곧 나올 그녀의 책이 미국, 그중에서도 워싱턴 권력의 중심 가까이에서 살면서 실제로 그 권력을 행사한 여성들에 관한 것이라는 사실이 흥미로웠어요.
translations_sent.17-17: 책 제목은 『더 이스트 윙』인데, 지난 90년간의 영부인들과 그들을 위해 일한 여성들, 그러니까 영부인의 역할과 이미지, 나아가 그들이 미칠 수 있는 영향력을 형성하도록 도운 사람들에 관한 이야기입니다.
translations_sent.18-18: 엘리너 루스벨트부터 멜라니아 트럼프까지, 영향력과 국제 관계의 이야기이고, 워싱턴에서 출발해 전 세계로, 냉전 시대부터 오늘날의 이란 전쟁까지 이어집니다.
translations_sent.19-19: 늘 그렇듯, 제 서면 노트에서 이 대화 너머의 배경 설명을 보실 수 있고, 링크는 쇼 노트에 있습니다.
translations_sent.20-20: 아자데와 저는 대화하는 내내, 영부인들이 전통적으로 사무실을 두었던 실제 이스트 윙이 트럼프 대통령의 새 연회장을 짓기 위해 철거되었다는 점을 의식하고 있었어요.
translations_sent.23-23: 아자데 무아베니가 뉴욕 스튜디오에 와서 저와 나눈 이야기입니다.
translations_sent.24-24: 아자데, 이런 시점에 당신의 폭넓은 생각이 궁금해요. 올해는 정말 격변의 한 해였으니까요.
translations_sent.26-26: 사실 저는 이란이 아주 조용하다고 생각해서 이 책 프로젝트를 맡았어요.
translations_sent.27-27: 제 주제를 다른 환경에서 탐구해 보자 싶어서 시작했죠.
translations_sent.32-32: 네. 처음에 영부인들과 그 참모들의 이야기에 관심을 갖게 된 계기가 뭐였나요?
translations_sent.33-33: 오랫동안 마음속에서 무르익던 주제였나요, 아니면 시작하게 된 특별한 순간이 있었나요?
translations_sent.34-34: 특별한 순간이라기보다는, 똑같은 접근법을 다른 맥락에서 이미 써본 경험이 있었어요.
translations_sent.35-35: 그전에 레바논에서 일하면서, 유엔이 주요 정치 지도자와 군벌, 각 종파의 큰 지도자들의 아내들을 한자리에 모아 레바논 분쟁을 완화하려던 계획에 대한 보고서를 썼어요.
translations_sent.36-36: 그러니까 아내들에게 초점을 맞추고 그들을 영향력 있는 존재로 인식한 거죠.
translations_sent.37-37: 그러다 뉴욕에서 일을 맡아 미국에 오게 됐고, 미국을 배경으로 한 작업이 필요했어요.
translations_sent.39-39: 그래서 여기서 권력 있는 거물 남성들의 아내들은 뭘 하고 있을까 생각했죠.
translations_sent.40-40: 그런데 이들이 정치적인 관점에서는 별로 다뤄지지 않는다는 걸 알게 됐어요.
translations_sent.41-41: 유명인처럼 다뤄지거나, 물론 전기가 있기는 하지만, 군주제에서 왕대비를 바라보듯 보는 시각은 거의 없었죠.
translations_sent.42-42: 왕좌와의 가족 관계를 통해 큰 권력을 갖게 되는 거예요.
translations_sent.43-43: 대통령직 안에, 핵심 자리에 있는 거죠.
translations_sent.44-44: 그리고 참모들을 앞세운 방식도 마음에 들어요. 그들은 막후에 있어서 훨씬 더 가려져 있으니까요.
translations_sent.45-45: 역사 속에서 그들은 완전히 주목받지 못했다고 생각해요. 대통령 비서실장들은 슈퍼스타라서 다큐멘터리도 있고 책도 있고, 비서실장이 어떻다 하는 전설도 있고, 자리가 대대로 이어지고 모임도 갖고, 대통령직을 돌리는 엔진으로서 관심의 대상이 되죠.
translations_sent.46-46: 그리고 그들은 대체로 공로도 인정받고 싶어 했어요.
translations_sent.47-47: 자신들의 영향력을 내세웠죠. 반면 영부인 주변의 여성들은 초반에 말씀하셨듯 그럴 가능성이 훨씬 낮고요.
translations_sent.49-49: 그들 중 많은 분을 인터뷰하기가 아주 어려웠어요. 이건 누구의 아이디어였냐고 묻는 게요.
translations_sent.52-52: 그러면 이렇게 말하세요. '음, 사실 저였지만…' 하면서도 결국 주인공인 영부인에게 공을 돌리려 해요.
translations_sent.53-53: 백악관 비서실장들과는 전혀 다르게 아주 신중하죠.
translations_sent.54-54: 그리고 그게 부분적으로는, 이야기하시는 초창기에 그들이 사교 비서로 고용되고 그 일이 정치적이거나 외교적이기보다 의례적이거나 겉치레로 여겨졌기 때문인가요?
translations_sent.55-55: 분명 그런 면이 있어요. 직함이 그들이 행사하는 영향력과 실제 하는 일을 반영하지 못하니까요.
translations_sent.56-56: 사교 비서관도 여전히 사교 비서관이라고 불리지만, 실제로는 모금과 정치, 외교를 다루는 자리예요.
translations_sent.57-57: 그러니 직함이 영향력을 가린 건 분명하죠.
translations_sent.58-58: 60년대와 70년대에 행정부 안에서 역할을 갖고 대통령 팀, 국내정책회의에 함께 앉기까지는 오랜 싸움이 필요했어요.
translations_sent.59-59: 행정부 운영에 참여하고 직함을 하는 일에 맞추려는 그런 흐름이 있었죠.
translations_sent.60-60: 하지만 그 이후에도 영부인을 위해 일하는 여성들 사이에는 존중하고 보호하고 신중하려는 태도가 몸에 배어 있다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.62-62: 수지 와일스가 독보적으로 강력한 위치에 있고요.
translations_sent.64-64: 그녀가 최초라는 것도 대단하고, 그것도 이 모든 민주적 규범을 깨뜨리고 있는 이번 정권에서 최초라는 게 더 놀랍죠.
translations_sent.66-66: 그런데도 그녀는 트럼프가 둔 비서실장 중 가장 유능하지만, 여성 의제를 추진하려고 거기 있다고는 보지 않아요. 반면 영부인의 비서실장과 참모들은 수십 년간 그게 자신들이 있는 이유의 일부라고 느꼈죠.
translations_sent.67-67: 아자데, 책 제목이 『더 이스트 윙』인데, 영부인 집무실이 있는 백악관 부분인 실제 이스트 윙이 잔해 더미가 된 바로 그 시점에 책이 나온다는 점이 정말 인상적이에요.
translations_sent.68-68: 책을 쓰는 중에 그 일이 벌어져서 저도 꽤 충격이었어요. 전혀 예상하지 못했거든요.
translations_sent.69-69: 저는 케네디 시대와 레이디 버드 존슨 시대까지 거슬러 올라가, 수년간 영부인들을 위해 일한 연로하고 훌륭한 여성들을 모두 인터뷰하기로 했는데, 이스트 윙 건물 자체가 위험에 처할 거라고는 상상도 못 했어요.
translations_sent.70-70: 조사의 맨 마지막에 하려고 아껴뒀는데, 완전히 철거돼 버렸죠.
translations_sent.72-72: 당신은 그걸 백악관 연회장 계획보다 더 큰 문제로, 영부인이라는 역할 자체에 대한 모욕으로 보는 쪽인가요?
translations_sent.73-73: 과거에 영부인들을 위해 일했던 여성들 중 많은 이들이 분명 그렇게 느꼈다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.74-74: 그들은 무시당했다고 느꼈어요. 이스트 윙은 그들의 사무실과 동의어나 다름없으니까요.
translations_sent.75-75: 그리고 그곳은 여성사의 바다 같은 곳이었죠.
translations_sent.76-76: 나중에 알았는데, 재키 케네디 시대부터 백악관 관리를 맡아온 백악관역사협회가 돌아다니며 그들이 일했던 모든 사무실을 거의 고고학적으로 사진을 찍어 보존해 두었더라고요.
translations_sent.77-77: 하지만 그 방식은, 공지도 없었고 공개 협의도 없었고 아무도 몰랐다는 점에서 문제라고 생각해요.
translations_sent.78-78: 그러니까 대중은 불도저가 건물을 들이받는 충격적인 이미지가 소셜 미디어에 올라오고서야 알게 됐잖아요.
translations_sent.79-79: 대중이 그 소식을 접한 방식에는 거의 폭력성이 느껴졌고, 백악관 역사에서 여성들에게 이 장소가 갖는 깊은 중요성에 둔감해 보였어요.
translations_sent.80-80: 멜라니아 트럼프에게 미리 의견을 구했는지는 알려진 게 있나요?
translations_sent.81-81: 그녀가 이 계획을 괜찮게 여기고, 자기 사무실이 다른 곳에 있는 걸 기꺼워한다고 보세요?
translations_sent.83-83: 그녀가 이걸 못마땅해했다는 사실이 보도로 드러나거나 인정된 적이 있어요.
translations_sent.85-85: 그녀는 이 계획을 옹호하고 나선 적이 단 한 번도 없어요. 연회장이 필요하다는 걸 이해하고 대통령의 계획을 지지한다고 볼 만한 방식으로는 전혀요.
translations_sent.86-86: 이 프로젝트에 자신의 지지와 신뢰도를 실어준 적이 없죠.
translations_sent.87-87: 이번에 두 번째로 영부인 역할을 맡으면서 예전과는 다른 영부인이 되었다는 느낌이 드시나요? 워싱턴에는 실제로 얼마나 있나요?
translations_sent.88-88: 제 생각에는 그녀가 실제로 관저에 들어와 자리를 잡기까지 꽤 여러 달이 걸렸어요.
translations_sent.89-89: 두 번째 임기는 첫 번째와 완전히 다르다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.93-93: 다큐멘터리 '멜라니아'에서 보면, 그녀는 두 번째 임기가 달라야 한다는 점을 아주 잘 인식하고 있어요.
translations_sent.94-94: 카메라 앞에서 이스트윙 사무실에서 일할 여성들을 직접 면접하면서, 한쪽 눈썹을 살짝 올리고 이렇게 묻죠. 내 두 번째 임기 사무실은 첫 번째와 어떻게 달라야 한다고 생각하나요?
translations_sent.95-95: 그러니까 관저에 자주 머물지는 않는다고 알려져 있지만, 훨씬 더 신중하고 계획적으로 움직여요.
translations_sent.101-101: 딥페이크와 리벤지 포르노를 범죄로 규정하는 '테이크 잇 다운 법'을 통과시키는 데 힘을 보탰어요. 의회에서 초당적으로 처리된 법안인데, 특히 젊은 여성들에게 분명히 영향을 미치는 문제죠.
translations_sent.102-102: 영부인이 의회에서 정말 중요한 법안을 통과시킨 건 아주 오랜만이라고 생각해요.
translations_sent.103-103: 그래서 그녀가 부분적으로는 오해받고 있다고 봐요.
translations_sent.104-104: 그녀는 이른바 주류 언론의 관심을 피하는데, 언론이 자신을 깎아내리고 진지하게 대하지 않는다고 생각하기 때문이에요.
translations_sent.105-105: 그리고 대중은 그녀가 시간을 쏟고 있는, 실제로 꽤 의미 있는 일들을 잘 모른다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.106-106: 당신이 '이스트윙'에서 들려주는 이야기는 물론 훨씬 길어요. 125년이 넘는 세월을 다루고, 영부인들뿐 아니라 그들을 위해 일한 여성들까지 아우르는 또 하나의 여성사로 그려내죠.
translations_sent.107-107: 처음으로 거슬러 올라가면, 1930년대의 엘리너 루스벨트가 있죠.
translations_sent.108-108: 새로운 방식으로 길을 열었고, 아무도 무시할 수 없는 영부인이 된 사람이요?
translations_sent.109-109: 맞아요, 대통령의 영향력 있는 동반자, 미국의 병폐를 읽어내는 해석자, 나라를 비추는 거울이라는 역할을 사실상 만들어낸 사람이에요.
translations_sent.114-114: 여성 기자들만 참석하는 기자회견을 열었는데, 여성 기자들이 1면에 기사를 싣고 편집국에서 진지하게 인정받길 바랐기 때문이에요.
translations_sent.116-116: 하지만 사실상 완전히 혼자, 직원 한 명 말비나 톰슨의 도움만으로 해냈어요. 이 이야기에서 중요한 인물인데, 둘이 한 팀이었거든요. 그러니 엘리너 루스벨트가 어떻게 엘리너 루스벨트일 수 있었을까요?
translations_sent.119-119: 2차 세계대전 이후 국제 질서의 일부였고, 그 질서 전체를 만든 사람 중 하나였죠.
translations_sent.120-120: 그런데 흥미로운 건, 60년 뒤 힐러리 클린턴이 영부인으로 백악관에 들어갈 때 엘리너 루스벨트가 그녀의 롤모델이었다는 거예요.
translations_sent.121-121: 그런 모습으로 활동할 수 있다고 생각했던 거죠.
translations_sent.122-122: 그런데 90년대의 미국은 그럴 준비가 안 돼 있었어요.
translations_sent.124-124: 어쩌면 지금도 준비가 안 됐다고 할 수 있겠고요.
translations_sent.126-126: 엘리너 루스벨트는 물론 그 시대의 인물이었어요.
translations_sent.127-127: 2차 세계대전과 대공황을 겪던 나라의 상황이 있었으니까요.
translations_sent.129-129: 90년대에 힐러리 클린턴은 정치적 야심이 매우 큰 의료 개혁 의제를 밀어붙였는데, 미국인들은 영부인이 정치적 야심과 신념을 감추고 누그러뜨리는 것, 심지어 대통령의 의제를 위해서도 그러는 걸 기대했기 때문에 그런 방식은 예상 밖이었던 거죠.
translations_sent.133-133: 힐러리 클린턴의 의료 개혁 경험 이후 영부인들이 배운 건, 이렇게 해야 한다는 거였다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.136-136: 자신들이 하는 일이 어떻게 보이도록 만드는 서사 전체가 필요했죠.
translations_sent.139-139: 미셸 오바마가 성공적인 사례라고 생각해요. 어린이 비만이라는 미국인의 건강 문제를 입법적으로까지 바꾸고 싶어 했지만, 백악관 텃밭을 가꾸고 나라 전체를 더 건강한 생활 방식으로 이끄는 것처럼 보이게 접근했거든요.
translations_sent.141-141: 건강하게 먹자는 건 실제 의료 제도를 건드리고 미국의 그 시스템에 맞서는 것에 비하면 안전한 주제잖아요.
translations_sent.143-143: 그런 점에서 보면 멜라니아 트럼프가 좀 더 용감하다고 볼 수도 있겠네요.
translations_sent.144-144: 어떤 면에서는 좀 더 용감하다고 할 수 있죠.
translations_sent.145-145: 레이건 시대까지만 해도 영부인들은 공화당이든 민주당이든 초당적으로, 남편의 선거에 위험이 되지 않는 선에서 여성 평등과 여성의 권리, 이 나라에서 여성의 역할과 관련된 사업과 정치적 사안을 맡을 수 있었어요.
translations_sent.147-147: 팻 닉슨은 더 많은 여성이 연방 정부에 임명되도록 하는 데 중요한 역할을 했고요.
translations_sent.148-148: 90년대에는 미국이 변하고 있었고, 복음주의 기독교와 종교가 부상하면서 전통적인 성 역할이 전에 없던 방식으로 정치의 한 요소가 됐어요.
translations_sent.149-149: 그래서 영부인이 사업과 정치적 활동에서 무엇에 집중하고 무엇을 시도할 수 있는지가 크게 제약됐죠.
translations_sent.151-151: 결국 영부인들은 늘 자기 시대의 맥락 안에서 움직여야 해요.
translations_sent.152-152: 또 다른 아주 유명한 영부인을 짚어보고 싶어요. 그녀에 대해 잘 알려지지 않은 면을 당신이 보여주고 있다고 생각해서요.
translations_sent.153-153: 재키 케네디는 스타일과 매력, 예술에 대한 사랑으로 유명하죠.
translations_sent.154-154: 그런데 그녀도 외교적 성과가 있었다는 걸 보여주시죠.
translations_sent.155-155: 당대 최고의 슈퍼스타였고 미국의 여왕처럼 기억되는 사람이죠, 카멜롯의.
translations_sent.156-156: 맞아요, 그녀의 놀라운 외교적 야심과 감수성, 영리함은 그녀의 이야기에서 거의 잊혀 있다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.157-157: 그녀는 사교 담당 비서이자 공보 비서인 티시 볼드리지와 긴밀히 일했는데, 볼드리지 역시 외교관이 되고 싶었지만 60년대라서 외교관으로 들어갈 수 없었어요.
translations_sent.158-158: 그래서 두 사람은 아주 섬세한 방식으로, 정치적 접대를 냉전 시기 케네디 행정부 외교 정책의 한 부분으로 만들었죠.
translations_sent.160-160: 재키는 미국의 관계를 완전히 바꿔놓았어요. 특히 인도와의 관계요. 네루 총리가 케네디 행정부를 아주 멀리하고 있었거든요.
translations_sent.161-161: 케네디를 젊고 세련된 멋쟁이 정도로 생각했던 것 같아요.
translations_sent.162-162: 케네디를 그렇게 진지하게 받아들이진 않았지만, 재키 케네디와 그녀의 여동생에게는 정말 끌렸어요.
translations_sent.163-163: 그래서 재키는 미국 정부에 의해 사실상 인도와 파키스탄 특사로 파견돼요.
translations_sent.164-164: 그리고 재키는 그곳에 가서 전 세계에 보도된 매혹적인 순방을 해냅니다.
translations_sent.165-165: 네루는 그 뒤로도 줄곧 집무실에 그녀의 사진을 두었고요.
translations_sent.167-167: 양국 관계를 굳히는 역할을 한 사람이 바로 재키였어요.
translations_sent.168-168: 흥미롭네요. 그리고 저는 책에서 다루신 내용 중 하나와 개인적으로 인연이 있는데요, 재키 케네디가 인도와 파키스탄에 가기 전에 파키스탄 대통령 아유브 칸이 워싱턴을 아주 화려하게 방문했잖아요.
translations_sent.171-171: 그때 아유브 칸의 영부인 역할은 그의 딸이 맡았어요.
translations_sent.172-172: 그 시기에는 딸이 영부인 역할을 했죠.
translations_sent.173-173: 그 마운트버넌 만찬 사진들을 찾아봤는데, 아유브 칸의 딸 나심이 사리를 입고 있더라고요.
translations_sent.174-174: 우리 할머니가 그분에게 사리 입는 법을 가르쳐 주신 분이에요.
translations_sent.175-175: 그러니까 파키스탄 영부인 역할을 준비하는 걸 도와주신 거죠.
translations_sent.176-176: 역사학자들과 영부인 연구자들 사이에서 지금도 기억되는 만찬이에요.
translations_sent.177-177: 역대 국빈 만찬 중에서 가장 상징적이고 정교하고 창의적인, 그야말로 최고의 볼거리였어요.
translations_sent.178-178: 해질녘에 포토맥강을 따라 배를 타고 마운트버넌까지 내려갔거든요.
translations_sent.181-181: 그 뒤로 그런 만찬은 한 번도 없었죠.
translations_sent.182-182: 대단하네요. 아자데, 이제 이 모든 걸 바라보는 이란계 미국인으로서의 시각에 대해 좀 이야기하고 싶어요. 본인의 뿌리에 대해서도 글을 쓰셨잖아요.
translations_sent.183-183: 중동 현지에서, 그리고 중동에 대해 25년 동안 취재해 오셨고요.
translations_sent.184-184: 이 책에서 두 분의 세계가 겹치는 순간이 있다고 생각하는데요, 재키 케네디가 한때 백악관에 온 이란 황후에게 거의 빛을 잃을 뻔했잖아요.
translations_sent.188-188: 당시 파라 황후는 재키 다음가는, 어쩌면 재키와 나란히 세계에서 가장 유명하고 세련된 왕족이자 퍼스트.
translations_sent.190-190: 그래서 샤와 황후가 워싱턴에 왔을 때 두 사람 사이에 일종의 스타일 대결이 벌어졌죠.
translations_sent.191-191: 케네디 대통령도 재키에게 농담을 했어요. 보석을 꺼내야겠다고요.
translations_sent.192-192: 황후가 당신보다 돋보이지 않게 해야 한다고요.
translations_sent.193-193: 그래서 두 사람 모두 각자의 시대에 자기 역할을 훌륭히 해냈고, 자국의 영광을 걸고 누가 무대 위에서 가장 빛나는 여성인지 세계의 시선을 받았다는 점이 흥미로웠어요.
translations_sent.194-194: 물론 이란으로서는 지금과 전혀 다른 시대였죠.
translations_sent.195-195: 그럼 이제 현재로 와서, 올해 이란과 미국 사이에 벌어진 이 놀라운 일들에 대해 이야기해 봅시다.
translations_sent.196-196: 분석하셔야 할 뿐 아니라 직접 마음으로도 느끼실 것 같아요.
translations_sent.197-197: 올해 벌어진 일들을 지켜보면서 예상하지 못했던 것 중에 무엇을 알게 되셨나요?
translations_sent.198-198: 저는 1월에 이란 사람들이 거리로 나올 거라고는 예상하지 못했어요.
translations_sent.200-200: 그렇게까지 정권에 맞서 나설 거라곤 생각 못 했죠.
translations_sent.201-201: 제가 이란을 취재한 지 벌써 30년 가까이 돼 가거든요.
translations_sent.202-202: 물론 이란 사람들은 아주 오랫동안 좌절하고 가난하고 분노해 왔고, 나름의 시민 불복종 운동으로 더 많은 시민적, 사회적 자유의 공간을 스스로 만들어 냈어요. 이란의 복장 규정을 사실상 끝내버린 '여성, 생명, 자유' 운동이 그 예고요.
translations_sent.203-204: 하지만 망명 중인 왕세자 레자 팔라비의 호소에 사람들이 응답하리라고는 생각하지 못했어요. 우리는 수년간 그를 취재해 왔고, 특히 이라크 전쟁을 취재한 사람들은 디아스포라의 역할을 정치인들이 지나치게 부풀려 상상할 수 있다는 걸 봤거든요. 군사적이든 아니든 고국의 변화를 위한 구상에 디아스포라 지도자를 기대하는 건 아주 위험할 수 있고요.
translations_sent.205-205: 사람들이 그렇게 나와서 전국 도시의 거리를 가득 메울 거라고는 예상하지 못했어요.
translations_sent.207-207: 그럼 다른 상황이었다면 1월의 그 움직임이 어디까지 커질 수 있었다고 보시나요?
translations_sent.208-208: 아주 좋은 질문이에요. 그 사이의 몇 주를 우리가 거의 잊고 있는데, 이란은 불과 48시간 만에 끔찍한 학살을 겪으면서 아주 빠르게 상황이 바뀌었거든요.
translations_sent.209-209: 숫자에는 이견이 있지만, 5천, 6천, 7천 명이라는 설명만 해도 엄청난 수의 사망자예요.
translations_sent.211-211: 훨씬 더 일찍 어떤 형태로든 군사 개입이나 최고지도자 암살, 혹은 전쟁 쪽으로의 움직임이 있었다면 이슬람 공화국이 정말 휘청했을지도 모른다고 생각해요. 사람들이.
translations_sent.213-213: 가장자리에 서 있었고, 모든 게 무너질 수도 있어 보였어요.
translations_sent.214-215: 하지만 그 사이의 몇 주 동안 사람들은 잔혹 행위의 규모를 알게 되었고 그게 두려움을 주었어요. 이 나라는 생존자들의 기억 속에 전례가 없는 학살이라는 깊은 트라우마를 겪었고, 그걸 감당하면서 체제와의 관계와 그 이후를 어떻게 받아들이고 생각해야 할지 고민하고 있었는데, 거기에 이 전쟁이 닥친 거죠.
translations_sent.216-216: 트럼프 대통령이 그 시위 당시에 도움이 가고 있다고 말했으니까요.
translations_sent.217-217: 그 사이 몇 주 동안 분위기가 바뀌었다는 말씀이시군요. 그래도 여전히, 사람들이 자국 정부에 아무리 반감이 있어도 외부 세력에게 폭격당하는 건 도저히 용납할 수 없는 일일 수 있다는 현실이 있고요.
translations_sent.219-219: 그는 도움이 가고 있다고 약속했지만 실제로는 오지 않았어요.
translations_sent.221-221: 사람들이 결국 그걸 원했을지는 저도 모르겠어요. 공격과 외세의 개입으로 정권이나 체제가 바뀌는 것에 대해서는 어디서든 사람들이 깊이 복잡한 심경일 테니까요.
translations_sent.222-222: 하지만 다른 길이 없다고 본 사람들도 많았어요. 이슬람 공화국의 보안 기구가 너무 큰 권력을 쥐고 있고 너무 억압적이어서, 외부의 도움 없이는 그걸 몰아내고 나라를 현재의 교착 상태에서 벗어나게 할 방법이 없다고요.
translations_sent.223-223: 그런데 전쟁은 군사 시설과 정권의 표적만 치는 참수 작전에 그치지 않았어요.
translations_sent.224-224: 아주 빠르게 이란 전체를 겨냥한 전쟁이 되어버렸죠.
translations_sent.227-227: 처음에는 이게 우리를 구해 줄지도 모른다고 생각했던 많은 사람들이, 이게 정권만이 아니라 나라 전체를 향한 전쟁이라는 걸 알게 된 거예요.
translations_sent.228-228: 그럼 최근에 그곳에 가셨을 때, 지난번보다 정권이 더 강해졌다고 느끼셨나요?
translations_sent.229-229: 4월과 5월 이후에 사람들이 체제에 보내던 신뢰를 계속 보내려는 의지는 지금 시들고 있다고 생각해요.

translations_sent.239-239: 그래서 지금은 분위기가 다시 분노와 좌절 쪽으로 돌아섰다고 생각해요.

translations_sent.244-244: 그리고 이 정권은 전쟁은 어떻게든 일으킬 수 있어도 평화는 가져다줄 수 없을 것처럼 보이죠.
translations_sent.245-245: 레자 팔레비가 여전히 그 적임자가 될 수 있다고 보세요?
translations_sent.246-246: 미래의 지도자가 될 수 있을까요, 아니면 그럴 기회는 이미 지나갔을까요?

translations_sent.250-250: 왜 그런가요? 그는 한 번도 해내지 못했어요.

translations_sent.256-256: 그것도 아주 노골적인 방식이어서 사람들이 불안해하고 등을 돌리게 됐다고 생각해요. 결국 사람들이 그에게 기대했던 카리스마와 리더십, 공감 능력으로 그 순간을 붙잡지 못했어요.
translations_sent.257-257: 그래서 그는 밖에서 파괴를 거들기만 하는 사람으로 비쳤다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.258-258: 이 지역 전반에 대한 생각도 듣고 싶어요. 이란만 취재하신 게 아니라 2000년대 초 이라크 전쟁 이후의 상황, 이른바 아랍의 봄, ISIS의 부상까지 지켜보셨으니까요.
translations_sent.259-259: ISIS에 합류한 여성들에 대한 책도 쓰셨고요.
translations_sent.260-260: 이슬람 혁명 시기, 그러니까 여성들이 호메이니를 권좌에 올리는 데 함께했던 때부터 이 지역 여성들의 변화, 혹은 변화 없음을 어떻게 설명하시겠어요?

translations_sent.263: 그리고 그건 종종 여성의 권리와 세속적 규범을 내세웠던 세속 독재자들에 대한 반발이나 반작용이었어요.
translations_sent.264-264: 그런 것들이 그들의 권위주의적 기풍의 일부로 여겨졌으니까요.
translations_sent.265-265: 그 부분을 조금 더 설명해 주셨으면 해요. 튀니지나 바샤르 알아사드 같은 곳을 떠올려 보면, 이슬람교도이면서도 세속적인 지도자들인데 정치적 권리는 거기서 나오지 않으니까, 정말 인상적이거든요.

translations_sent.269-269: 이슬람주의와 지하드주의를요. 결국 그렇게 아주 퇴행적이고 배타적인 정신까지 받아들여서 그 정권들을 무너뜨리려 했어요.
translations_sent.270-270: 그건 부분적으로, 좀 너드 같은 얘기가 되고 있긴 한데요 미셸, 지역마다 여성들이 이런 무장 운동에 참여한 건 운동이 성공하면 자신들도 포함되고, 협상 테이블에 한자리를 차지하고, 새 질서의 일부가 될 거라고 상상했기 때문이거든요.
translations_sent.271-271: 하지만 현실은 그렇게 되지 않았고, 그래서 아랍 세계의 많은 여성이 이슬람국가에 합류한 거예요.
translations_sent.273-273: 그건 어쩌면 설명하기가 더 어려운데요, 영국을 떠날 때 열다섯 살이었던 샤미마 베검처럼 아주 어린 여성들도 있었어요.

translations_sent.293-293: 그러니까 이 십대들은 자기 역할이 있을 것 같은 이 일종의 유토피아에 가담하도록 꼬임에 넘어간 거라고 생각해요.
translations_sent.294-294: 마무리로 중동과 미국 관계를 좀 더 넓게 이야기해 볼게요, 아자데. 이 지역에서 미국이 앞으로도 주둔할지, 기지는 어떻게 될지, 더 넓게는 미국이 얼마나 계속 관여할지에 대한 논의와 논쟁이 많거든요.
translations_sent.295-295: 도널드 트럼프는 더 이상 전쟁은 없다고 말한 대통령이었잖아요.
translations_sent.296-296: 그런데 정작 미국을 중동의 또 다른 전쟁으로 끌고 들어간 사람이 그예요.

translations_sent.303-303: 옛 체제는 아주 큰 비용을 치르면서 걸프 아랍 국가들에 안보를 제공하기로 한 건데, 실제로는 오히려 이들을 지독히 취약하게 만들었으니까요.

translations_sent.305-305: 그럼 그 압력이 걸프 국가들 쪽에서 나올 거라고 보세요? 카타르의 대형 기지 같은 곳 말이에요.

translations_sent.312-312: UAE를 취약하게 만든다면 무슨 쓸모가 있겠어요?

translations_sent.319-319: 그러니까 보호비를 내면서도 더 이상 보호받지 못하는 셈이죠.

translations_sent.322-322: 그러니까, 기지들이 점점 줄어들다가 결국 사라지는 걸 보게 될까요?

translations_sent.340-340: 하지만 결국 이란 사람들의 안녕에 책임이 있는 건 미국이 아니에요.
